cells.tense: Right now the heart is open and the hands are off the controls.
cells.ask: Say one thing out loud that you don't know yet, to the person you'd most want to hear it. Leave it there without fixing it after.
cells.core:
You're open right now, and you're not bracing for anything. That's rare. Most people only feel something once they've decided what it is, but you can sit in the not-yet — a thing starting to move in you before it has a name. It's not blankness. It's attention without a grip on it.

It sits well in this clearing. Instead of rushing to fill the bare room, you're standing in it. The pull toward what might be felt is active, and it isn't dragging you anywhere yet. Keep it that way a little longer — let the space stay bare past the point where it feels uncomfortable. That's not stalling. That's the part most people skip.
cells.sheetLine: You're open to something new before you know what it is.
cells.verb: Staying open to feeling something new before there is anything in particular to feel
cells.place: A room being cleared out, where the floor is bare and nothing has been put back yet

cells.tense: In a few weeks you will already be rehearsing how this is going to feel.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're clearing and take one small act of ending it — cancel it, delete it, hand it back. One act, not the whole goodbye.
cells.core:
You're reaching forward to feel what isn't here yet. You've already started imagining how it will land, what you'll feel when it's done, what comes after — and you're gripping that feeling before it has arrived. The openness that should be soft is clenched around an outcome you can't write.

That grip costs you the actual moment, which is the only one you can feel in. It also keeps you from doing the one thing that would settle it. Make one ending real, in the world, with your hands. Not the speech, not the whole farewell — cancel the thing, return the thing. That gives the feeling something to arrive into, instead of a future to brace against.

cells.tense: Something opened in you once, and you have been watching its doorway from a distance since.
cells.ask: Set a five-minute timer and ask one person one true question about how they are. Listen to the answer to the end without planning your reply.
cells.core:
You started to feel something and you didn't come in. You can still remember when it seemed possible to let a feeling be felt, and you stepped back from it. Since then you've kept your distance and called that distance being careful.

The space ahead of you looks like bare fear rather than room. But the way back in is small — you don't have to rush through anything. Be a beginner again for one thing. Ask someone a real question and let their answer be new to you. That's the smallest way of letting something arrive, and it gets the current moving again, in you and in whoever is with you.

cells.tense: You are already feeling your way through this clearing, and you're telling it as weather.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're already open to that you've been calling circumstance — tell one person, plainly, that you've started to feel something about it.
cells.core:
You're already open to what's next. It shows in how you talk about what ended — not cold, not finished, already turning toward what's ahead. You feel it first and describe it second, and you keep describing it as if it were happening to you.

It isn't. The openness is yours; the name on it isn't. That's the only piece missing: saying out loud that this is you receiving something, not the situation doing it to you. Pick one thing you've been treating as circumstance and speak as the one who's already let it in. That naming costs nothing and changes which way the rest of it flows, for you and for whoever hears it.
